blocking_issues.location: EN/PT-BR section 'The 1872 census: what the 1.51 million figure shows' / 'O censo de 1872: o que o total de 1,51 milhão demonstra'
blocking_issues.issue: Both editions call 10,112,061 a 'later-adjusted' census population and pair it with 1,510,806 enslaved persons, while other official IBGE tabulations give 9,930,478 total and 1,510,806 enslaved. Both national totals appear in historical/official materials but reflect different compilations or vintages; the text does not identify which denominator it uses, why it is 'later-adjusted', or reconcile it with the other widely used total. This affects the enslaved share and historical comparability.
evidence: EN: 'first nationwide Brazilian census recorded a later-adjusted population of 10,112,061 ... including 1,510,806 classified as enslaved'; PT-BR paired claim.
IBGE 2009 Censo 2010 historical note reports 9,930,478 total and 1,510,806 enslaved (https://censo2010.ibge.gov.br/images/pdf/censo2010/revista/vtc12_web.pdf).

IBGE 2019 historical timeline displays 10,112,061 (https://nada.ibge.gov.br/media/com_mediaibge/arquivos/47ad07161ac72b90ad0b2387ab2dda34.pdf). Reconciliation needed, not an unsupported declaration that either number is fabricated.

blocking_issues.issue: The carrier chart is a legitimate sourced series, but the report needs a second distinct quantitative comparison. The geographic `map` is a qualitative region card including 'Asia and Middle East' although the plotted Atlantic dataset excludes those regions; its caveat prevents outright falsification but the surrounding text must make clear it is a conceptual scope comparison rather than a measured Atlantic flow map. evidence: SlaveVoyages estimates table confirms 12,521,337 total embarkations and carrier categories Portugal/Brazil 5,848,266, Great Britain 3,259,441, France 1,381,404 and Spain/Uruguay 1,061,524 (https://legacy.slavevoyages.org/assessment/estimates).
Current map explicitly says 'qualitative, not measured geographic routes'; it is not evidence of measured interregional flow quantities.

contrary_evidence: The Atlantic embarkation database does not measure arrivals alive or non-Atlantic slave systems.
The ILO modern slavery estimate uses modelled prevalence categories, not a legal chattel-slavery census.
Present-day inequality also depends on later migration, land policy, education, industrialisation and discrimination; no single causal share is identified.
limitations: Historical census national total differs across official historical tabulations and must be reconciled; no claim that one is definitively wrong.
